The 2024 survey *Complementary Recommendation in E-commerce* distinguishes substitutes from complements and highlights asymmetric relationships, coexistence of both relations, and varying complement strength. This supports auditing relationships between specific item pairs rather than equating semantic similarity or co-purchase with compatibility. A similar product can be an alternative without being redundant for that user. [Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16135)

Evidence sufficiency should be checked separately from relevance. *Sufficient Context* (ICLR 2025) finds that models frequently answer incorrectly when retrieved context lacks necessary information; combining sufficiency signals with confidence improves selective answering. Product attribute research likewise acknowledges that titles and descriptions cannot establish every missing attribute. These findings support an explicit “insufficient evidence” outcome rather than converting missing specifications into compatibility conflicts. [Sufficient Context](https://research.google/pubs/sufficient-context-a-new-lens-on-retrieval-augmented-generation-systems/), [Attribute prediction](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-industry.18.pdf)

Suggested adaptation: extract product type, intended use, model identifiers, connectors, dimensions, and explicit compatibility statements, retaining supporting text spans. Label pairs as supported complement, likely substitute, explicit conflict, or insufficient evidence; require affirmative evidence for conflicts and keep substitution separate from user-level redundancy. An accessory purchase does not establish ownership of its associated equipment. Manually check a stratified sample across all four categories, including ambiguous titles, missing specifications, and explicit exclusions; report extraction precision, relation confusion, unsupported-claim rate, and accuracy versus abstention coverage. These are proposed audit procedures, not validated results or replacements for validation HR@10.
